questions.prompt: For a single-pole op-amp \(A(j\omega)=\dfrac{A_0}{1+j\omega/\omega_{-3dB}}\), what is the phase of \(A\) at frequencies far above \(\omega_{-3dB}\)?
questions.explanation: For \(\omega\gg\omega_{-3dB}\), \(A\approx\dfrac{\omega_u}{j\omega}\) (reader Eq. 18.8): dividing by \(j\) is a \(-90^\circ\) phase shift. It is exactly \(-45^\circ\) only AT the pole, and a single pole can never reach \(-180^\circ\).

questions.prompt: An op-amp has \(A_0=2\times10^5\) and \(f_{-3dB}=5\ \mathrm{Hz}\). What is \(|A|\) at 10 kHz?
questions.explanation:
\(f_u=A_0f_{-3dB}=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Far above the pole \(|A|\approx f_u/f=10^6/10^4=100\).
Exact: \(\dfrac{2\times10^5}{\sqrt{1+2000^2}}=100\). A '106 dB' op-amp has only 40 dB of gain at 10 kHz.

questions.prompt: An inverting amplifier (\(R_1\), \(R_2\)) uses a single-pole op-amp with unity-gain frequency \(\omega_u\). Its closed-loop bandwidth is approximately
questions.explanation:
Reader Eq. 18.15: \(\omega_0=\dfrac{A_0\omega_{-3dB}}{1+R_2/R_1}=\dfrac{\omega_u}{1+R_2/R_1}\). The factor \(1+R_2/R_1=1/f\) (the 'noise gain') appears, not the signal gain \(R_2/R_1\); for large gains the two are nearly equal, which is why the reader concludes GBW \(\approx\omega_u\) (Eq. 18.16).
• Multiplying would make high gain faster, which is backwards.
• Feedback does extend the bandwidth beyond the open-loop pole.

questions.prompt: Same amplifier (\(R_2/R_1=4\)), op-amp \(f_u=2\ \mathrm{MHz}\). What is the closed-loop \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) frequency, in kHz?
questions.explanation:
\(f_0=\dfrac{f_u}{1+R_2/R_1}=\dfrac{2\ \mathrm{MHz}}{5}=400\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
Common mistake: dividing by 4 (500 kHz); the noise gain \(1+R_2/R_1=5\) sets the bandwidth.

questions.prompt: For the inverting amplifier (\(R_2/R_1=4\), closed-loop pole \(f_0=400\ \mathrm{kHz}\)), what is the phase of \(v_o/v_s\) at \(f=f_0\)?
options: \(+135^\circ\) (equivalently \(-225^\circ\)): \(180^\circ\) from the inversion plus \(-45^\circ\) from the pole
questions.explanation:
\(G(j\omega)\approx-\dfrac{R_2}{R_1}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+j\omega/\omega_0}\) (reader Eq. 18.14). The minus sign is \(\pm180^\circ\); at \(\omega=\omega_0\) the pole adds \(-45^\circ\). Total \(180^\circ-45^\circ=135^\circ\).
• \(-45^\circ\) forgets the inversion.
• \(180^\circ\) is the low-frequency phase.
• \(-90^\circ\) is the pole's phase far above \(\omega_0\), still without the inversion.

questions.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has closed-loop gain \(1/f\) and bandwidth \(f\cdot\omega_u\). Well ABOVE that bandwidth, how does its closed-loop magnitude behave?
options: It drops at \(-40\ \mathrm{dB/decade}\), twice as fast as the op-amp
It rises back toward the open-loop DC gain
It merges with the open-loop curve \(|A|\approx\omega_u/\omega\): the loop gain is \(<1\), so feedback no longer acts
questions.explanation: \(A_{CL}=\dfrac{A}{1+Af}\). Above \(f\omega_u\), \(|Af|<1\) and \(A_{CL}\approx A\): the closed-loop curve lies on top of the open-loop \(-20\ \mathrm{dB/decade}\) line (reader Fig. 17.17 and 18.9). One pole, one slope: no \(-40\) dB/decade.

questions.prompt: Gotcha check: an inverting amplifier with \(R_2/R_1=100\) is built from an op-amp with only \(A_0=1000\). What is its actual DC gain?
questions.explanation:
\(G=-\dfrac{100}{1+101/1000}=-\dfrac{100}{1.101}=-90.83\), about 9% below \(-100\).
The loop gain is only \(T=A_0/(1+R_2/R_1)=1000/101\approx9.9\), not 1000. A high closed-loop gain eats the loop gain. Common mistake: assuming the error is \(1/A_0=0.1\%\).

questions.prompt: Two amplifiers both have \(|\text{gain}|=1\): a follower and an inverting stage with \(R_2=R_1\). Same op-amp, \(f_u=10\ \mathrm{MHz}\). How do their bandwidths compare?
options: Both about 10 MHz, since both have unity gain
Follower about 10 MHz; inverting about 5 MHz, because its noise gain \(1+R_2/R_1\) is 2
Follower about 5 MHz; inverting about 10 MHz
questions.explanation: Bandwidth \(=f_u\cdot f\). The follower has \(f=1\). The inverting stage returns only \(f=R_1/(R_1+R_2)=1/2\) of the output to \(V^-\), so its bandwidth is \(f_u/2=5\ \mathrm{MHz}\) even though \(|\text{gain}|=1\). The signal gain and the feedback factor differ in the inverting topology.

questions.prompt: Preview of slewing. The inverting amplifier with \(R_2/R_1=4\) and \(f_u=2\ \mathrm{MHz}\) is driven by a SMALL input step. Its response is a single-pole exponential with \(\tau=1/\omega_0\). What is the 10%–90% rise time, \(2.2\tau\), in µs?
questions.explanation:
\(f_0=400\ \mathrm{kHz}\), so \(\tau=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\cdot4\times10^5}=0.398\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) and \(t_r=2.2\tau=0.875\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
That's the linear (small-signal) speed. For large steps the op-amp may hit its slew-rate limit and ramp more slowly; the slew skill compares the two.
questions.figure_alt: Small input step and an exponential output.

questions.prompt: Preview of datasheets. A datasheet (the ADA4891 discussed in the reader) lists GBW \(=240\ \mathrm{MHz}\) and open-loop gain \(=66\ \mathrm{dB}\). Assuming a single dominant pole, where is the open-loop \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) frequency, in kHz?
questions.explanation:
\(A_0=10^{66/20}=1995\). Then \(f_{-3dB}=\dfrac{GBW}{A_0}=\dfrac{240\ \mathrm{MHz}}{1995}=120.3\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
Datasheets usually give GBW and DC gain, not the pole: you back it out with the single-pole model. Common mistake: using \(10^{66/10}\).

questions.prompt: Preview of slew rate. A follower uses an op-amp with \(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\) and a maximum output slope of \(0.5\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\). A \(0.1\ \mathrm{V}\) step is applied. What happens?
options: It settles purely exponentially, since \(0.1\ \mathrm{V}\) is a small step
The linear response would start at \(0.63\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\), above the limit, so the output first ramps at \(0.5\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\), then settles exponentially
The output rises instantly, since the follower has gain 1
questions.explanation: The linear model gives \(v_o=V(1-e^{-\omega_ut})\) with initial slope \(V\omega_u=0.1\times2\pi\times10^6=0.628\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\). That exceeds \(0.5\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\), so the start is slope-limited (a ramp); once the remaining slope falls below the limit, the exponential takes over (reader Fig. 18.13–18.15). 'Small' is relative to \(SR/\omega_u=0.08\ \mathrm{V}\).
